samples.answer:
For a U.S.-based online business, the **best payment processor depends mainly on your platform, sales model, and volume**. My practical shortlist:

| Best for | Processor | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Most online businesses** | **Stripe** | Excellent APIs, hosted checkout, subscriptions, invoices, fraud tools, wallets, and international payment methods |
| **Shopify stores** | **Shopify Payments** | Simplest integration and avoids Shopify’s extra third-party transaction fees |
| **Online + in-person sales** | **Square** | Strong POS, invoices, payment links, appointments, and basic online-store tools |
| **Adding a trusted wallet** | **PayPal** | Many customers recognize it and may prefer PayPal, Venmo, or Pay Later |
| **Large/global businesses** | **Adyen** | Global acquiring, local payment methods, multi-currency support, and interchange-plus pricing |
| **SaaS or digital products worldwide** | **Paddle** | Acts as Merchant of Record and handles payments, subscriptions, tax compliance, fraud, and chargebacks |

## My recommendations

### 1. Stripe — best overall default

Choose Stripe if you have a custom website, SaaS product, marketplace, membership business, or developer-supported checkout. It offers hosted Checkout and Payment Links as well as APIs, subscriptions, invoicing, tax tools, fraud prevention, and more than 100 payment methods. Its standard U.S. domestic-card pricing is currently **2.9% + $0.30 per successful transaction**, with custom pricing available for larger volumes. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** flexibility, subscriptions, custom workflows, startups, software businesses.  
**Downside:** you may need technical help, and extra products such as Billing, Tax, or advanced fraud tools can add fees.

### 2. Shopify Payments — best if you use Shopify

If your store runs on Shopify, start with Shopify Payments unless you have a specific reason not to. It is integrated into Shopify’s checkout, payouts, orders, refunds, and reporting. Shopify also says that third-party transaction fees may apply if you use another payment provider instead. Rates vary by Shopify plan, card type, and country, so check your admin account for the exact rate. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** physical-product ecommerce on Shopify.  
**Downside:** less portable than using a standalone processor; Shopify plan and third-party fees can materially affect your total cost.

### 3. Square — best for businesses that also sell offline

Square is a strong option for businesses that take payments online and in person—such as retailers, salons, consultants, instructors, restaurants, and service businesses. It combines online payments with point-of-sale software, invoices, payment links, and hardware. Square’s rates vary by payment type and plan, so distinguish online, in-person, manually entered, invoice, and Afterpay transactions when comparing costs. ([api.squareup.com](https://api.squareup.com/help/us/en/article/5068-what-are-square-s-fees?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** omnichannel small businesses that value simplicity over deep customization.  
**Downside:** its online and ecommerce capabilities are generally less flexible than Stripe’s.

### 4. PayPal — best as an additional checkout option

PayPal is often worth offering alongside another processor because some customers trust it or want to use PayPal balance, Venmo, or Pay Later. PayPal’s current U.S. commercial rates depend on the product: standard card payments are listed at **2.99% plus a fixed fee**, while PayPal Checkout and some other products use different rates. International and Pay Later transactions cost more. ([paypal.com](https://www.paypal.com/us/business/paypal-business-fees?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** increasing payment choice and conversion.  
**Downside:** I generally would not make PayPal your only processor unless its ecosystem is central to your business.

### 5. Adyen — best for high-volume or international businesses

Adyen is designed more for established companies than very small businesses. It supports global and local payment methods, flexible settlement currencies, and interchange-plus pricing. Its pricing is generally a fixed processing fee plus the payment method’s fee, with no setup or monthly fee listed; implementation and underwriting are more enterprise-oriented than Stripe or Square. ([adyen.com](https://www.adyen.com/pricing?pix=6f_0_0&utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** international expansion, high volume, sophisticated payments teams.  
**Downside:** more complex setup and usually not worth it for a small or early-stage business.

### 6. Paddle — best for SaaS and downloadable digital products

Paddle is a **Merchant of Record**, meaning it takes responsibility for much of the payment, tax, compliance, fraud, chargeback, and billing burden. Its standard pay-as-you-go price is currently **5% + $0.50 per checkout transaction**, so the rate is higher than basic card processing, but it can be worthwhile if you sell globally and want to avoid managing sales tax/VAT/GST complexity yourself. ([paddle.com](https://www.paddle.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** SaaS, software licenses, apps, subscriptions, and digital products sold internationally.  
**Downside:** higher headline fees and less control than using Stripe directly.

## Simple decision rule

- **Custom website or SaaS:** Stripe  
- **Shopify store:** Shopify Payments  
- **Store plus physical location or appointments:** Square  
- **Need PayPal/Venmo customer choice:** Add PayPal  
- **High-volume international operation:** Adyen  
- **Global digital products with tax complexity:** Paddle  

## What to compare before deciding

Do not compare only the headline percentage. Check:

1. **Total effective rate:** percentage fee, fixed fee, international surcharge, currency conversion, and monthly product fees.
2. **Chargeback fees and reserves:** especially for subscriptions, travel, supplements, tickets, or high-risk products.
3. **Payout timing:** how quickly funds reach your bank account.
4. **Recurring billing:** retries, card updates, prorations, cancellations, and refunds.
5. **Payment methods:** Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal, Venmo, ACH, buy-now-pay-later, and local methods.
6. **Data portability:** whether you can export customers, payment tokens, and transaction history.
7. **Tax responsibility:** particularly if you sell across U.S. states or internationally.

**Bottom line:** For most new online businesses, I would start with **Stripe**, use **Shopify Payments** if the business is on Shopify, and add **PayPal** if customers are likely to expect it.

| **PayPal Business** | Small businesses and consumer-facing stores | Customers can pay in hundreds of local currencies; U.S. business accounts can hold balances in up to **21 foreign currencies** | Strong international consumer recognition, PayPal wallets, cards, Apple Pay, Google Pay, and international transactions ([paypal.com](https://www.paypal.com/us/brc/article/how-to-accept-foreign-currency-with-your-business-account?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Adyen** | Medium-to-large businesses and global enterprises | Supports processing and settlement across multiple currencies; exact payout options vary by acquiring region | Global and local payment methods, local acquiring, online and in-person payments, multi-country operations ([adyen.com](https://www.adyen.com/online-payments?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Airwallex** | Global businesses needing payments plus multi-currency accounts | Collects payments in **130+ currencies** | Global cards, bank transfers, local payment methods, multi-currency wallet balances, and settlement in supported currencies ([airwallex.com](https://www.airwallex.com/docs/billing/supported-currencies?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Paddle** | SaaS, software, apps, and digital products | Supports **30+ payment currencies** and multiple payout currencies | Handles checkout, payments, currency conversion, and sales-tax/VAT obligations as a merchant-of-record provider ([developer.paddle.com](https://developer.paddle.com/concepts/sell/supported-currencies/?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Checkout.com** | Enterprise e-commerce and marketplaces | Supports multiple payment currencies, with availability dependent on business country and setup | International cards and local payment methods; settlement currencies vary by country ([support.checkout.com](https://support.checkout.com/hc/en-us/articles/14327144437906-Supported-payment-methods-and-currencies-in-the-US?utm_source=openai)) |

### Quick recommendation

- **Most businesses:** Stripe  
- **Small business wanting a familiar international wallet:** PayPal  
- **Global enterprise with local payment methods:** Adyen or Checkout.com  
- **International operations and multi-currency balances:** Airwallex  
- **SaaS or digital goods where tax compliance is important:** Paddle  

One important distinction: **accepting a customer’s currency is not the same as receiving payouts in that currency**. A provider may let you charge customers in EUR, GBP, JPY, or other currencies but convert the funds before depositing them. Availability also depends on your business’s registration country, customer location, payment method, and industry.

**My default recommendation: Stripe Billing.**

It is the best fit for most subscription businesses that need:

- Recurring card charges
- Automatic retries for failed renewals
- Smart retry timing or custom retry rules
- Customer emails and payment-method update flows
- Subscription states such as `past_due`, `unpaid`, and `canceled`
- Hosted checkout and customer self-service tools
- Webhooks for provisioning or suspending access

Stripe Billing includes machine-learning-based **Smart Retries**, custom retry schedules, failed-payment reminders, and recovery reporting. Stripe says Smart Retries recover an average of 57% of recurring payments that initially failed, although your results will vary. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/billing/features?utm_source=openai))

### When I would choose something else

| Situation | Better choice |
|---|---|
| You want maximum control and a strong developer ecosystem | **Stripe Billing** |
| You sell digital products globally and want someone else to handle sales tax/VAT and merchant-of-record responsibilities | **Paddle Billing** |
| PayPal is especially important to your customers or you already use PayPal infrastructure | **Braintree** |
| You mainly need payment processing rather than a full subscription-management system | A gateway plus a dedicated billing platform such as Chargebee or Recurly |

Paddle is particularly attractive for international SaaS because its Retain system automatically retries failed renewal payments and sends recovery emails, with a configurable dunning window. The tradeoff is less control over payment and billing behavior than with Stripe. ([paddle.com](https://www.paddle.com/help/profitwell-metrics/retain/how-it-works/retain-payment-recovery-how-it-works-retry-cadence?utm_source=openai))

Braintree does support automatic retries, but its built-in model is more limited and configuration-oriented: it provides three initial automated retries, followed by additional retry behavior that you configure. It also warns that some hard declines should not be retried. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/recurring-billing/recurring-advanced-settings?utm_source=openai))

### Recommended Stripe setup

For a typical subscription product, configure:

1. **Stripe Checkout or Payment Element** for signup.
2. **Stripe Billing subscriptions** with `charge_automatically`.
3. **Smart Retries** for renewal failures.
4. A recovery policy such as:
   - keep the subscription `past_due` during recovery,
   - suspend product access after the retry window,
   - cancel or mark unpaid after a defined period.
5. Webhooks for:
   - `invoice.payment_failed`
   - `invoice.payment_succeeded`
   - `customer.subscription.updated`
   - `customer.subscription.deleted`
6. Automatic customer emails and a secure “Update payment method” page.
7. Card Account Updater and support for alternative methods such as ACH where appropriate.

Stripe subscriptions become `past_due` when a required payment fails, and after configured retry attempts can be left past due, marked unpaid, or canceled. ([docs.stripe.com](https://docs.stripe.com/api/subscriptions/object?lang=&utm_source=openai))

**Bottom line:** Choose **Stripe Billing** unless your main priority is outsourcing global tax/compliance—in which case choose **Paddle**. Don’t build your own retry engine initially; use the provider’s retry logic and only add custom handling around access suspension, customer messaging, and analytics.

For most freelancers in the U.S., the best setup is:

## **Use Stripe Invoicing or Payment Links**

Stripe is usually the strongest all-around choice because clients can pay by credit/debit card or digital wallet without creating an account, and you can send a professional invoice or simple payment link. Stripe’s standard U.S. online-card rate is currently **2.9% + $0.30 per successful domestic card transaction**; ACH Direct Debit is **0.8%, capped at $5**. Payment Links require no website or coding. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/pricing))

### Recommended workflow

1. Create a free Stripe account.
2. Connect your business bank account.
3. Send an itemized invoice with:
   - Scope of work
   - Due date
   - Deposit or milestone amount
   - Late-payment terms
   - Card and ACH payment options
4. Require a deposit—commonly **30–50%**—before beginning work.
5. Save the invoice, receipt, contract, and payment confirmation for your records.

## Good alternatives

| Service | Best for | Typical U.S. online card pricing |
|---|---|---:|
| **Stripe** | Professional invoices, payment links, recurring retainers, website integrations | **2.9% + $0.30** |
| **Square** | Freelancers who also accept in-person payments or want simple invoicing | **2.9% + $0.30** for online payments; no monthly charge on the cited standard setup ([squareup.com](https://squareup.com/us/en/the-bottom-line/managing-your-finances/payment-gateway)) |
| **PayPal Business** | Clients who specifically prefer PayPal, Venmo, or PayPal Pay Later | Invoices: **2.99% + $0.49** for cards/Apple Pay; PayPal or Venmo payments are **3.49% + $0.49** ([paypal.com](https://www.paypal.com/us/business/accept-payments/invoice?gh_jid=4602865)) |
| **QuickBooks Payments** | You already use QuickBooks and want payments reconciled with bookkeeping | Convenient, but compare its current processing rates with Stripe before choosing |

## My practical recommendation

- **Most online freelancers:** Stripe invoice with card and ACH enabled.
- **Freelancers who meet clients in person:** Square.
- **Clients who insist on PayPal/Venmo:** Maintain a PayPal Business account as a secondary option.
- **Large invoices:** Encourage ACH to reduce processing fees.
- **Recurring work:** Use recurring invoices or automatic card payments, but obtain clear written authorization.

Avoid asking clients to email card numbers or entering card details manually whenever possible. Use hosted checkout pages or payment links so the processor handles the sensitive card information. Also remember that card payments can still be disputed; keep signed agreements, approved deliverables, emails, and proof of delivery.

## Short answer

**Stripe Connect is the best default choice** for a high-volume marketplace paying many sellers—especially if you want fast implementation, strong seller onboarding, automated KYC/compliance workflows, flexible split payments, reporting, refunds, disputes, and global payouts in one system. Stripe supports direct charges, destination charges, and splitting one payment among multiple sellers. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/connect/features?utm_source=openai))

### Choose Adyen for Platforms instead if:

- You are a large enterprise with a complex, international operation.
- You need both **online and in-person payments**.
- You want sophisticated settlement, balance-account, and reconciliation controls.
- You have the engineering and payments team to manage a more involved integration.

Adyen supports split payments across multiple seller balance accounts, configurable settlement models, managed or custom payouts, and detailed control over commission, processing fees, refunds, and chargebacks. ([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/platforms/quickstart-guide/payments/?utm_source=openai))

## Practical comparison

| Requirement | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Fastest launch and developer-friendly APIs | **Stripe Connect** |
| Large seller base with automated onboarding and payouts | **Stripe Connect** |
| International enterprise marketplace | **Adyen for Platforms** |
| Online + physical/omnichannel commerce | **Adyen** |
| Complex split, reserve, settlement, and chargeback allocation rules | **Adyen** |
| Strongest general-purpose marketplace ecosystem | **Stripe Connect** |
| PayPal/Venmo acceptance is strategically important | Add **PayPal/Braintree** alongside the core platform, if commercially justified |

Stripe advertises support for onboarding connected accounts, global payouts, scheduled or instant payouts, tax-form support, and payment flows involving multiple parties. Its current Connect pricing also varies materially depending on whether Stripe or your platform handles payment pricing, risk, and payout economics—so high-volume pricing should be negotiated rather than evaluated from the standard card rate alone. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/connect/pricing?utm_source=openai))

## My recommendation

Start with **Stripe Connect using Express or Custom connected accounts**, unless you already have a sophisticated payments team. Before signing, negotiate:

1. **Interchange-plus or volume pricing**
2. Cross-border and FX fees
3. Instant-payout pricing
4. Chargeback and negative-balance liability
5. Reserve requirements
6. Seller-country and payout-country coverage
7. Data export and reconciliation capabilities
8. Contractual payout and account-support SLAs

One important issue is **loss liability**: depending on the Connect charge type and account configuration, your marketplace may still bear exposure when sellers cannot cover refunds or chargebacks. Stripe explicitly documents scenarios where losses can be recovered from the platform. ([support.stripe.com](https://support.stripe.com/questions/reserves-for-connect-platforms-and-connected-accounts?utm_source=openai))

**Bottom line:**  
- **Most marketplaces:** Stripe Connect.  
- **Very large, global, omnichannel marketplaces with sophisticated finance operations:** Adyen for Platforms.  
- **Do not choose based only on headline processing rates**; payout fees, FX, reserves, chargeback liability, onboarding coverage, and reconciliation usually matter more at scale.

Assuming you’re in the **U.S.**, there isn’t one universally cheapest processor—the best choice depends on whether you take payments **in person, online, by invoice, or via ACH**, plus your average transaction size.

## Best low-fee options

| Processor | Published standard fees | Best for |
|---|---:|---|
| **Helcim** | Interchange + **0.40% + 8¢** in person; interchange + **0.50% + 25¢** online for businesses processing under $50,000/month | Lowest potential card-processing cost |
| **Square Free** | **2.6% + 15¢** in person; **2.9% + 30¢** online/API; **3.3% + 30¢** invoices | Small or occasional sellers wanting no monthly subscription |
| **Stripe** | **2.9% + 30¢** for domestic online cards | Online businesses, subscriptions, websites, and apps |
| **PayPal** | **2.99% + 49¢** for standard card payments; **3.49% + 49¢** for PayPal Checkout; ACH via PayPal Online Services is **0.8%, capped at $5** | Businesses that need PayPal/Venmo checkout or invoices |

Helcim uses interchange-plus pricing, so the exact cost varies by card type. Its published margin is generally lower than flat-rate processors, and it says typical effective rates are near or below 2% in person and below 2.5% online. ([helcim.com](https://www.helcim.com/pricing/?hcmSprt=1))

Square Free has no monthly subscription cost, but its invoice and online-link rates are higher than its in-person rate. Square also offers lower in-person rates on its paid Plus and Premium plans, though the subscription cost can offset those savings for very small sellers. ([api.squareup.com](https://api.squareup.com/help/us/en/article/5068-what-are-square-s-fees))

Stripe’s standard online rate is 2.9% + 30¢ with no setup or monthly fees, making it competitive and straightforward for online sales. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/pricing)) PayPal’s rates are generally less attractive for ordinary card payments, but it can still be worthwhile if customers specifically prefer PayPal or Venmo. ([paypal.com](https://www.paypal.com/us/business/paypal-business-fees))

## My practical recommendation

- **Lowest fees overall:** **Helcim**, especially if you process at least a few thousand dollars monthly and can handle variable interchange pricing.
- **Best for a small brick-and-mortar business:** **Square Free** for simplicity and no monthly commitment.

Before switching, confirm **what kind of decline you’re seeing**. A payment provider can’t override an issuer decline, and repeated retries can worsen your decline ratio or incur network retry fees. Separate:

- **Issuer declines** — the customer’s bank rejected the payment.
- **Gateway/provider rejections** — your provider’s AVS, CVV, fraud, velocity, 3DS, or configuration rules blocked it.
- **Technical failures** — timeout, processor outage, malformed payment request, or token problem.
- **Recoverable recurring failures** — expired/reissued cards or temporary insufficient funds.

Braintree’s documentation, for example, explicitly distinguishes bank declines from gateway rejections and warns that repeated attempts can inflate decline rates. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/transactions/declines?utm_source=openai))

- **International or high-volume store:** compare **Adyen** and **Checkout.com**.

1. **Authorization rate by issuer country, card network, debit/credit, and decline code**
2. **False-decline monitoring and merchant-level reporting**
3. **Network tokens**
4. **Real-time and batch card-account updater**
5. **Smart retry rules that respect Visa/Mastercard retry guidance**
6. **Selective 3DS—not blanket 3DS**
7. **Dynamic routing or multiple acquiring connections**
8. **Wallet support: Apple Pay, Google Pay, and PayPal**
9. **Clear distinction between issuer declines and provider risk blocks**
10. **Migration of vaulted cards, subscriptions, customer IDs, refunds, and dispute history**

1. Export the last 30–90 days of failed payments.
2. Group them by exact response code and reason.
3. Identify whether declines cluster by country, issuer, BIN, browser, device, 3DS status, AVS/CVV result, or order value.
4. Run the replacement provider in a controlled **5–10% traffic pilot**.
5. Compare approval rate, fraud rate, chargebacks, checkout latency, refunds, support burden, and net revenue—not just raw declines.
6. Keep the current provider active until recurring tokens and refund workflows have been validated.

3. **Loss responsibility**  
   Who bears card chargebacks, negative seller balances, fraud losses, refunds after payout, and seller insolvency?

4. **Reserve and rolling-hold policy**

   Test the actual KYC flow with your seller demographics. A provider with theoretically broader coverage may still produce poor seller conversion.

7. **API and operational limits**  
   Check rate limits, webhook guarantees, idempotency, bulk payout APIs, reporting latency, API versioning, and support escalation.

- **Under roughly enterprise scale or prioritizing speed:** Stripe Connect.

If your store runs on Shopify, start with Shopify Payments unless you have a specific reason not to. It avoids unnecessary complexity and integrates directly with Shopify checkout and orders. It is most compelling for software, subscriptions, apps, and other digital products—not ordinary physical-product ecommerce. ([paddle.com](https://www.paddle.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

Compare these before choosing:

- **Average order value:** Fixed fees hurt more on low-priced products.
- **Subscriptions:** Look for failed-payment retries, card updating, prorations, and customer self-service.
- **International sales:** Check currency-conversion, cross-border, payout, and local-payment-method fees.
- **Chargebacks:** Review dispute fees and protection programs.
- **Payout holds:** Payment processors may reserve or delay funds, especially for new or high-risk businesses.
- **Refunds:** Some processors do not return the original processing fee when you refund a transaction.
- **Platform lock-in:** Shopify Payments and Square are convenient but more tied to their ecosystems.
- **Tax compliance:** A normal processor usually does not make you compliant with sales-tax obligations; a Merchant of Record such as Paddle is different.

- **Custom website or SaaS:** Stripe  
- **Shopify store:** Shopify Payments, plus PayPal  
- **Online and physical sales:** Square  
- **Need PayPal/Venmo/Pay Later:** PayPal or Braintree  
- **Global digital products and subscriptions:** Paddle  
- **Marketplace or complex enterprise business:** Stripe Connect or an enterprise provider with custom pricing  

For many businesses, the best setup is **Stripe or Shopify Payments as the primary processor, with PayPal enabled as an additional checkout option**.

- You want to launch relatively quickly.

- You need to split one transaction among multiple recipients.

- You already operate at substantial enterprise scale.
- You need highly customized split-payment and balance-account logic.
- You have complex international acquiring, currencies, settlement, or treasury requirements.

Adyen’s platform model uses balance accounts, explicit split instructions, managed payouts, or custom payout timing, with detailed accounting and transfer webhooks. It is powerful, but generally involves a more enterprise-oriented implementation and sales process. ([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/marketplaces/process-payments/?utm_source=openai))

### Consider **Mangopay** if:

Your marketplace is especially EU-focused or needs wallet-based fund management, delayed release, complex transfers, or marketplace-specific payment flows. Mangopay positions its product around multi-seller marketplaces, wallets, split payments, and global payouts. ([docs.mangopay.com](https://docs.mangopay.com/guides/payouts?utm_source=openai))

### Consider **PayPal** if:

PayPal or Venmo acceptance is strategically important. For a marketplace, compare the **total payout and risk economics**, not just the card rate:

1. Payment processing fee  
2. Connected-account or platform fee  
3. ACH and debit-card payout fees  
4. International payout and FX costs  
5. Chargeback and refund liability  
6. Negative-balance responsibility  
7. Reserve requirements and payout delays  
8. KYC/KYB verification failure rates  
9. Seller onboarding conversion  
10. Reconciliation and reporting quality  
11. Tax-form support  
12. Support escalation for frozen or restricted seller accounts

Obtain a detailed quote and test results rather than relying on advertised averages. ([worldpay.com](https://www.worldpay.com/en/optimize-authorization-rates?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Braintree** | Stores that want PayPal plus cards in one integration | Worth considering if PayPal is important or you already use the PayPal ecosystem. It provides decline codes and Smart Retries, but its own documentation emphasizes that many declines originate with the customer’s bank, not Braintree. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/transactions/declines?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Shopify Payments** | Stores already running on Shopify | The lowest-friction option for Shopify merchants, with built-in fraud analysis and Shopify-specific checkout integration. It is not automatically a cure for issuer declines, and Shopify still holds merchants responsible for chargebacks. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/fraud-prevention?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Authorize.net** | Smaller U.S.-based businesses wanting conventional gateway support | A practical option for Shopify, WooCommerce, BigCommerce, Magento, and other platforms, with configurable fraud filters, recurring billing, card vaulting, wallets, PayPal, and eChecks. It is less focused than the enterprise providers on sophisticated global routing and authorization optimization. ([authorize.net](https://www.authorize.net/payments/ecommerce.html?utm_source=openai)) |

## My practical shortlist

- **Typical U.S. ecommerce store:** compare **Stripe**, **Braintree**, and your platform-native option—such as Shopify Payments.
- **International or rapidly scaling store:** compare **Adyen**, **Checkout.com**, and **Worldpay**.
- **Small business needing hands-on support and a conventional gateway:** include **Authorize.net**.
- **Subscription business:** prioritize account updaters, network tokens, stored-credential compliance, and decline-aware retries—not merely the headline transaction rate.

## Before switching, ask each provider to prove performance

Run a controlled pilot or parallel integration if possible. Require reporting by:

1. **Issuer response code and decline category**—hard decline, soft decline, fraud decline, authentication failure, gateway rejection, expired credential, etc.
2. **Approval rate**, both initial and after permitted recovery attempts.
3. **False-decline rate**, not just total decline rate.
4. **Approval by card brand, issuer country, customer country, device, order value, and subscription status.**
5. **Chargeback and fraud rate**, since simply approving more transactions can worsen losses.
6. Support for **network tokens, account updater, 3‑D Secure 2, wallet payments, AVS/CVC tuning, and intelligent retries**.
7. Data portability: whether you can migrate vaulted cards/tokens without forcing customers to re-enter payment details.

([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/industries/peak-season/risk-and-disputes/?utm_source=openai))

**Bottom line:** For most stores, start with a competitive test between **Stripe and Adyen** if you have meaningful volume, or **Stripe and your platform-native processor** if you are smaller. **Use Stripe Billing** unless you specifically want a merchant-of-record service.

- Customer self-service payment-method updates

- Flexible pricing, trials, coupons, prorations, usage-based billing, and webhooks

Stripe subscriptions can automatically charge customers on a recurring schedule, and its revenue-recovery tools retry failed payments based on signals intended to improve recovery rather than using a simple fixed schedule. | Situation | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Standard SaaS, memberships, content, or services | **Stripe Billing** |
| You sell digital products globally and want the provider to handle sales tax/VAT | **Paddle** |
| PayPal/Venmo acceptance is especially important | **Braintree** |
| Complex enterprise billing, multiple payment processors, or global acquiring optimization | **Adyen** or Stripe plus a dedicated billing platform |

### Choose Paddle instead if tax/compliance is the main concern

Paddle acts as the **merchant of record**, handling payment processing, sales tax/VAT collection and remittance, invoicing, and related compliance. It also includes automated dunning and card-retry functionality. This can significantly reduce operational work, though you generally give up some control and may pay more than using Stripe directly. ([paddle.com](https://www.paddle.com/help/sell/tax/how-paddle-handles-vat-on-your-behalf?utm_source=openai))

### Choose Braintree if PayPal matters

Braintree supports recurring billing with configurable automatic retries and account-updater functionality. It’s worth considering if a meaningful share of your customers will pay with PayPal, but its retry logic is more explicitly rule-based, and certain hard declines should not be retried. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/recurring-billing/recurring-advanced-settings?utm_source=openai))

Start with:

> **Stripe Checkout + Stripe Billing + Smart Retries + automatic card updates + Customer Portal**

Configure your system to:

1. Retry eligible soft declines automatically.
2. Email customers when payment fails.
3. Give them a one-click payment-update flow.
4. Keep the subscription `past_due` during recovery.
5. Cancel or suspend access only after your chosen retry window.
6. Listen to webhooks so product access matches payment status.
7. Avoid repeatedly retrying hard declines; card networks and processors impose retry restrictions. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/guides/optimizing-authorization-rates?utm_source=openai))

## Short answer

For **most U.S.-based, high-volume marketplaces paying many sellers**, I’d start with **Stripe Connect**. It offers the strongest combination of:

- Seller onboarding and KYC/KYB
- Split payments and platform commissions
- Scheduled or manual payouts
- Instant payouts
- Refunds, disputes, tax reporting, and reconciliation
- Global payments and payouts
- A mature API and embedded onboarding experience

Stripe supports multiple marketplace fund-flow models, including destination charges and splitting one buyer payment among multiple sellers. It also supports payout schedules from daily to monthly/manual and provides U.S. 1099 capabilities. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/connect/features?utm_source=openai))

## Best choice by situation

| Situation | Best fit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| New marketplace, primarily U.S., fast launch | **Stripe Connect** | Best overall developer experience and broad marketplace tooling |
| Large global enterprise with significant payment volume | **Adyen for Platforms** | Strong acquiring, local payment methods, risk controls, split payments, and payout orchestration |
| Marketplace needs wallet/escrow-like balances or complex fund flows | **Mangopay** | Wallet infrastructure is central to its product; supports receiving, holding, splitting, transferring, KYC/KYB, and payouts |
| Global sellers, many currencies, and FX optimization | **Airwallex for Platforms** | Strong cross-border payout coverage, multi-currency infrastructure, and can work alongside another primary PSP |
| Enterprise platform wanting negotiated economics and payment control | **Checkout.com** | Flexible platform-led model, custom commissions, automated splits, seller payouts, and enterprise support |
| PayPal/Venmo is essential for buyers or sellers | **PayPal Complete Payments / Multiparty** | Useful when PayPal network acceptance or payouts are strategically important |

Adyen supports seller onboarding, payments, custom or managed payouts, fraud controls, and reconciliation in one platform; it is generally more appropriate when you have enterprise-scale requirements and can support a more involved commercial and integration process. ([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/adyen-for-platforms-model?utm_source=openai))

Mangopay is particularly attractive when your marketplace needs a formal wallet/ledger model—for example, delayed settlement, buyer-to-seller transfers, complex split logic, or marketplace balances. Its payout flow is based on withdrawing funds from platform wallets to verified external bank accounts. ([docs.mangopay.com](https://docs.mangopay.com/guides/payouts?utm_source=openai))

Airwallex is worth considering if international payouts and FX are the main pain points. It supports marketplace splits, seller onboarding, payouts to more than 200 countries, and an “acquirer-agnostic” model in which another PSP can process the buyer payment while Airwallex handles seller payouts. ([airwallex.com](https://www.airwallex.com/docs/payments-for-platforms/use-cases/payments-for-marketplaces?utm_source=openai))

## My practical recommendation

### Choose Stripe Connect if:

- You want to launch in weeks rather than quarters.
- Most sellers are in the U.S. or Stripe-supported countries.
- Sellers are businesses, contractors, creators, or service providers.
- You want Stripe to handle much of the onboarding, compliance, disputes, and tax infrastructure.
- Your payment flow is reasonably standard: buyer pays, marketplace takes a fee, seller receives the balance.

### Choose Adyen or Checkout.com if:

- You already process at substantial enterprise volume.
- Authorization rates and direct acquiring economics matter more than ease of implementation.
- You need sophisticated multi-region acquiring, local payment methods, and negotiated pricing.
- You have an experienced payments, risk, and reconciliation team.

### Choose Mangopay if:

- You need a ledger or wallet architecture.
- Funds may remain in seller balances before release.
- Your marketplace has complicated split, escrow-like, refund, or milestone workflows.
- You are especially focused on European marketplace infrastructure.

### Consider a two-provider architecture if:

- You want separate optimization for **payment acceptance** and **seller payouts**.
- You operate across many regions.
- You need redundancy or payment-routing flexibility.
- Your existing PSP is good at checkout but weak at global payouts.

Airwallex specifically supports using another PSP for acquiring while handling marketplace payouts, which can make it useful as a payout layer rather than a complete replacement. ([airwallex.com](https://www.airwallex.com/docs/payments-for-platforms/use-cases/payments-for-marketplaces?utm_source=openai))

## What matters more than headline processing rates

For a high-volume marketplace, evaluate these items in the contract and technical review:

1. **Who is liable for chargebacks and negative seller balances?**
2. **Can you delay payouts** until delivery, returns, fraud review, or a milestone?
3. **Can one payment be split among several sellers?**
4. **Can you debit sellers** for refunds, disputes, or adjustments?
5. **Which countries and seller types are supported?**
6. **How are reserves, rolling holds, and account closures handled?**
7. **What are the real payout costs**, including ACH, card, wire, FX, instant payout, and failed-payout fees?
8. **Can you reconcile payment, transfer, refund, dispute, and payout events reliably?**
9. **Who owns the seller relationship and seller data?**
10. **Can pricing be negotiated at your projected volume?**

At high volume, the lowest card-processing rate is often less important than payout failure rates, reserve policy, FX spreads, dispute handling, and the ability to reconcile thousands or millions of seller-level ledger entries.

## Bottom line

**Default recommendation: Stripe Connect.**  
**Enterprise/global alternative: Adyen for Platforms.**  
**Wallet-heavy or complex marketplace: Mangopay.**  
**Global payout and FX specialist: Airwallex.**

Before committing, run a commercial and operational bake-off using your real data: seller countries, average order value, refund rate, chargeback rate, payout frequency, currencies, and expected monthly GMV.

If legitimate cards are being declined, **switching providers may help—but first determine whether the failure is from the card issuer, your provider’s fraud rules, or the gateway/processor configuration.** A gateway rejection is different from an issuer authorization decline; the former can result from AVS/CVV rules, duplicate checks, fraud thresholds, or 3DS configuration. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/transactions/gateway-rejections/?utm_source=openai))

## Providers worth evaluating

| Provider | Best fit | Why consider it |
|---|---|---|
| **Stripe** | Startups, SaaS, subscriptions, and businesses wanting a fast integration | Offers Adaptive Acceptance, Smart Retries, card-account updater, network tokens, and issuer/network optimization features aimed at recovering legitimate declines. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/guides/optimizing-authorization-rates?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Adyen** | Larger or international retailers, omnichannel businesses, and merchants wanting more control | Supports network tokenization, real-time account updater, 3DS2, risk optimization, and routing-related optimization. Its real-time updater can retry a declined stored-card payment after obtaining updated card details. ([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/online-payments/tokenization/?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Braintree / PayPal** | Businesses that want cards plus PayPal/Venmo, or already use the PayPal ecosystem | Provides Smart Retries, account updater, network tokenization, 3DS, and payment-optimization features. Account Updater availability and supported cards depend on geography and setup, so confirm this during the sales process. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/account-updater?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Authorize.net** | Smaller U.S. merchants wanting a conventional gateway/merchant-account setup | Worth considering if you want to retain or choose your own acquiring bank. It supports card-on-file account updating and fraud filters, but it may require more configuration and processor coordination than Stripe or Braintree. ([authorize.net](https://www.authorize.net/content/dam/authorize/documents/standard_reseller_agreement.pdf?utm_source=openai)) |

### My practical shortlist

- **Most businesses:** run a controlled test with **Stripe and Braintree**.
- **High volume, international, or multi-region:** include **Adyen**.
- **Small U.S. store with an existing merchant account:** evaluate **Authorize.net** before undertaking a full platform migration.
- **Subscription business:** prioritize account updater, network tokens, intelligent retries, and clear decline-code reporting over headline transaction pricing.

## Before switching, require these capabilities

Ask each provider to demonstrate:

1. **Separate reporting for issuer declines, fraud blocks, gateway rejections, timeouts, and 3DS failures.**
2. **Network tokenization** and both real-time and batch account updater.
3. **Issuer-aware retry logic** that respects Visa/Mastercard retry limits rather than blindly resubmitting transactions. Stripe and Braintree both document restrictions on excessive retries. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/guides/optimizing-authorization-rates?utm_source=openai))
4. **Configurable AVS, CVV, and risk rules** so low-risk legitimate orders are not automatically blocked.
5. **3DS2 with a frictionless path**, rather than forcing every customer through a challenge.
6. **Multiple acquiring connections or intelligent routing**, particularly if you sell internationally.
7. **Token portability or a migration process** for saved cards. Adyen, for example, documents options for forwarding stored payment details or network tokens to PCI-compliant third parties. ([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/online-payments/tokenization/?utm_source=openai))
8. **Transparent decline data**, including the raw network response code and issuer advice—not just “card declined.”

## Do a pilot instead of switching blindly

For 2–4 weeks, route a representative slice of traffic through the candidate provider while keeping the existing provider active. Compare:

- authorization rate by issuer, card brand, country, device, and order value;
- false-positive fraud declines;
- 3DS completion rate;
- retry recovery rate;
- chargebacks and refunds;
- latency and timeout rate;
- total cost per successfully completed order.

Do not compare only the advertised processing fee. A provider charging slightly more per transaction may be cheaper if it produces materially more successful orders.

**Important:** If most failures are issuer declines such as insufficient funds, do-not-honor, suspected fraud, or card restrictions, changing providers may produce only a modest improvement. If failures are gateway rejections, excessive AVS/CVV rules, failed 3DS flows, stale card-on-file data, or poor retry handling, a provider change—or a configuration fix—can have a much larger effect.

Assuming you’re a U.S.-based online retailer, I’d shortlist these providers—but first determine whether the problem is actually your processor. A bank/issuer can decline a perfectly valid card based on its own fraud signals; however, your gateway can also reject transactions before they reach the bank because of AVS/CVV rules, fraud thresholds, account configuration, or authentication failures. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shopify-payments/transactions/declined-payments?utm_source=openai))

## Providers worth evaluating

### 1. **Stripe**
Best general-purpose replacement for most small and midsize e-commerce businesses.

Why consider it:

- Adaptive Acceptance and network-level optimization for soft declines
- Smart Retries for failed recurring payments
- Card Account Updater and network tokens to reduce failures after cards expire or are replaced
- Strong developer tools, analytics, wallets, and broad payment-method support ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/guides/optimizing-authorization-rates?utm_source=openai))

Stripe also offers an “Authorization Boost” product that it says recovers an average of 20% of false declines, though you should validate that claim against your own transaction mix. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/authorization-boost?utm_source=openai))

**Good fit:** Typical DTC store, SaaS, subscriptions, or a business wanting a relatively straightforward integration.

### 2. **Adyen**
Best for larger merchants, international sales, or businesses needing sophisticated risk and routing controls.

Adyen’s tools include:

- Risk-based 3-D Secure authentication
- Machine-learning risk decisions
- Custom allow/block/review rules
- Authentication optimization designed to reduce unnecessary customer challenges and improve issuer acceptance
- Performance analysis through Adyen Uplift ([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/online-payments/authentication?utm_source=openai))

**Good fit:** Higher volume, international customers, multiple currencies, complex fraud patterns, or an engineering team that can support a more involved implementation.

### 3. **Braintree**
Best if PayPal, Venmo, or stored-card billing is important.

Braintree supports:

- Network tokens
- Account Updater
- Automated and machine-learning-based retries
- Vaulted payment methods and recurring billing
- PayPal integration within the same broader ecosystem ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/guides/account-updater?utm_source=openai))

Be careful with retry configuration: repeated attempts on certain decline categories can trigger card-network fees or worsen the customer experience. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/articles/control-panel/transactions/declines?utm_source=openai))

**Good fit:** Subscription businesses, merchants already using PayPal, or stores that want a strong vault and recurring-billing setup.

### 4. **Worldpay**
Worth evaluating for high-volume or international businesses that want processor-led optimization and routing.

Worldpay advertises dynamic routing, machine-learning decisioning, account updating, and authorization analytics. It is more enterprise-oriented, so expect a sales-led process and negotiated pricing rather than a simple self-serve setup. ([worldpay.com](https://www.worldpay.com/en/optimize-authorization-rates?utm_source=openai))

**Good fit:** Large transaction volumes, multiple regions, complex acquiring needs, or a desire to negotiate processing economics.

### 5. **Shopify Payments**
If your store is on Shopify and the issue is partly checkout integration or gateway configuration, test Shopify Payments before moving platforms. Shopify says it automatically routes transactions to the processor most likely to authorize them. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shopify-payments/transactions/declined-payments?utm_source=openai))

That said, Shopify Payments will not eliminate issuer declines, and Shopify itself notes that banks—not Shopify—make many card-decline decisions. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/checkout-settings/troubleshooting-checkout-payments?utm_source=openai))

**Good fit:** Shopify merchants prioritizing simplicity, Shop Pay, and tight native integration.

## My practical recommendation

- **Small/midsize standard store:** Start with **Stripe**.
- **Subscriptions or PayPal-heavy audience:** Compare **Stripe vs. Braintree**.
- **International or high-volume store:** Run an RFP with **Adyen and Worldpay**, and include Stripe as a benchmark.
- **Shopify store:** Test **Shopify Payments vs. Stripe**, but only after reviewing whether Shopify’s fraud, AVS, and checkout settings are causing gateway rejections.

## Before switching, request this data

Ask your current provider for the last 60–90 days broken down by:

1. Issuer decline vs. gateway rejection  
2. Decline code and network response code  
3. AVS, CVV, fraud-rule, and 3-D Secure outcomes  
4. Card brand, country, issuer country, device, and wallet usage  
5. First payment vs. recurring payment  
6. Approval rate by customer segment and transaction type  

Then run a **two-to-four-week controlled pilot** with the same traffic mix. Compare:

- Authorization rate
- Checkout completion rate

4. Send a Stripe or Square invoice—not your bank or card details.

6. Keep payment confirmations and reconcile them with your accounting records.

**Stripe Connect is the best default choice** for a high-volume marketplace paying many sellers—especially if you want fast implementation, strong APIs, embedded seller onboarding, automated KYC/KYB, split payments, scheduled or instant payouts, and broad international coverage. | Processor | Best for | Main strengths | Main drawbacks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stripe Connect** | Most marketplaces and platforms | Fast integration; excellent developer tools; seller onboarding; split payments; global payouts; instant payouts; tax/reporting features | High-volume pricing must be negotiated; payout and platform fees can matter at scale |

Mangopay is particularly suited to platforms that need wallet-based money movement: funds are held in Mangopay wallets and paid out to verified external bank accounts, subject to KYC/KYB and risk controls. ([docs.mangopay.com](https://docs.mangopay.com/guides/payouts?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **Stripe Connect** if:

- You are primarily US-based or want to launch quickly.
- You want the lowest engineering and operational burden.
- Sellers are individuals, small businesses, freelancers, or service providers.
- You need embedded onboarding, automated verification, refunds, disputes, tax reporting, and payouts in one stack.
- Your marketplace may later add subscriptions, cards, financing, instant payouts, or other Stripe financial products.

([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/connect/pricing?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **Adyen for Platforms** if:

- You process very large volumes and payment economics are a major concern.
- You operate across many countries and need local acquiring or payment methods.
- You need sophisticated settlement, reconciliation, risk, or payout controls.
- You have an experienced payments/finance engineering team.
- You are willing to run a competitive procurement process and negotiate enterprise pricing.

Adyen offers both managed payouts—designed to reduce operational complexity—and custom scheduled or on-demand payouts with different transfer speeds. ([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/platforms/quickstart-guide/payouts?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **Mangopay** if:

- Your business model depends on wallet balances, escrow-like flows, delayed release of funds, or complex marketplace balances.
- You are heavily focused on Europe.
- You need more control over the internal funds ledger than a conventional connected-account model provides.

Before signing, compare these items using your actual transaction data:

1. **Total cost**, not just card processing: acquiring, cross-border, FX, refunds, chargebacks, payout fees, instant payouts, KYC checks, and account fees.
2. **Seller geography**: where sellers live, where their bank accounts are, and which currencies they need.
3. **Funds flow**: direct charges, destination charges, split payments, delayed settlement, escrow-like holds, and negative-balance handling.
4. **Liability**: who bears fraud, refunds, chargebacks, and seller insolvency risk.
5. **Onboarding conversion**: how many sellers abandon identity verification.
6. **Payout reliability**: bank-account verification, failed payouts, return handling, payout timing, and support.
7. **Reconciliation**: whether transaction, fee, refund, dispute, transfer, and payout records can be reconciled cleanly to your order ledger.
8. **Commercial terms**: volume tiers, reserves, rolling holds, minimums, termination rights, and whether you can use another processor later.

**Bottom line:** Start with **Stripe Connect** as the baseline, but run a pricing and capability bake-off against **Adyen for Platforms** if your annual payment volume is substantial or international. ([legal.helcim.com](https://legal.helcim.com/us/fee-disclosures/?utm_source=openai))

- **High-volume or international store:** run an RFP with **Adyen**, **Checkout.com**, and one other processor—not just a consumer-facing gateway.

Give each candidate a representative 30–60 day transaction sample and request:

1. Approval rate by card brand, issuing country, amount, and device.
2. “False decline” or fraud-block rate.
3. Breakdown of issuer declines versus gateway/risk declines.
4. Recovery rate for soft declines and failed recurring payments.
5. Support for network tokens, account updater, AVS/CVV, and 3-D Secure 2.
6. Whether they can provide a second acquiring route or intelligent routing.
7. Exact handling of retry limits and network retry fees.

Also run a **parallel A/B pilot** rather than switching all traffic immediately. Route a statistically meaningful portion of legitimate traffic to the candidate processor, compare approval rate and fraud/chargeback rate, and measure net recovered revenue—not just authorization percentage.

One important caveat: if the card issuer is rejecting the transaction, changing providers may not solve the problem. ### Choose **Stripe Connect** if:

- You want one integrated platform for checkout, seller onboarding, compliance, split payments, and payouts.
- You need to launch or iterate quickly.
- Your sellers are primarily in supported Stripe countries.
- You want flexible models such as:
  - platform-collects-then-transfers,
  - direct charges on sellers,
  - destination charges,
  - one payment split among multiple sellers.
- You want sellers to receive daily, weekly, manual, or instant payouts. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/connect?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **Adyen for Platforms** instead if:

- You already operate at substantial enterprise scale.
- Global acquiring and local payment methods are major priorities.
- You need detailed balance-account accounting and reconciliation.
- You want more control over payment routing, settlement, payout timing, risk management, and operational reporting. ([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/marketplaces/process-payments/?utm_source=openai))

## Important architecture issue

Do not evaluate only the card-processing rate. For a marketplace, the difficult parts are usually:

1. **Seller KYC/KYB and onboarding**
2. **Who is liable for refunds and chargebacks**
3. **Whether you can delay payouts until delivery or a return period expires**
4. **Splitting one payment among multiple sellers**
5. **Negative balances and seller reserves**
6. **Cross-border payouts and foreign exchange**
7. **Tax reporting**
8. **Reconciliation and ledger quality**
9. **Payout failure handling**
10. **Country and product restrictions**

For example, Stripe supports payout timing controls and can aggregate earnings before settlement, while Adyen explicitly models funds in balance accounts and applies split instructions to payments, captures, refunds, and fees. - **Best enterprise/global alternative:** Adyen for Platforms  
- **Best for wallet-heavy or complex marketplace fund flows:** Mangopay  
- **Best when PayPal/alternative payout methods are central:** PayPal/Hyperwallet  

Before selecting one, get custom quotes based on **gross payment volume, average transaction size, seller count, payout frequency, countries, currencies, chargeback rate, and required reserve/hold period**. In the U.S., **online payment processors commonly charge about 2.9%–3.5% plus $0.30 per successful card transaction**.

| Processor / method | Typical online fee |
|---|---:|
| **Stripe** domestic card | **2.9% + $0.30** |
| **Square** online API | **2.9% + $0.30** |
| **Square Payment Links** | **3.3% + $0.30** |
| **PayPal standard card payments** | **2.99% + fixed fee** |
| **PayPal Checkout** | **3.49% + fixed fee** |
| **ACH bank transfer** | Usually **about 0.8%–1%**, often capped |
| **Buy-now-pay-later** | Often **roughly 5%–6% + $0.30** |

([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

- Percentage fee: $2.90  
- Fixed fee: $0.30  
- **Total fee: $3.20**
- You receive approximately **$96.80**

For high-volume businesses, **interchange-plus pricing** can be cheaper than flat-rate pricing, but it is more complicated and usually negotiated. Ordinary small businesses generally budget around **3%–4% of online card sales** after the fixed per-transaction charge.

| **Stripe** | Most small-to-mid-sized stores; subscriptions; custom checkout | Strong authorization tooling, including Adaptive Acceptance, network tokens, account updater, and Smart Retries. ([stripe.com](https://stripe.com/guides/optimizing-authorization-rates?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Adyen** | Larger or international merchants | Good choice when you need global acquiring, multiple currencies/payment methods, network tokenization, account updater, and more control over risk and routing. Its network-token and account-updater features are documented as part of its tokenization stack. ([docs.adyen.com](https://docs.adyen.com/online-payments/tokenization/?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Braintree** | Stores that want cards plus PayPal, Venmo, and wallets | Supports network tokens, lifecycle updates, account updater, 3DS, and PayPal methods in one integration. It also offers payment orchestration for connecting multiple PSPs or acquirers. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/network-tokens/how-it-works?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Shopify Payments** | Stores already using Shopify | Worth testing before adding a separate gateway. Shopify says it automatically routes transactions to the processor most likely to authorize them, and its decline tooling exposes information from the issuing bank. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shopify-payments/transactions/declined-payments?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Checkout.com** | Enterprise or high-volume international commerce | Consider it if you have a payments team and need enterprise-level network-token, account-updater, and acceptance-optimization capabilities. Its own materials position these tools primarily for enterprise merchants. ([checkout.com](https://www.checkout.com/products/network-tokens?utm_source=openai)) |

### My practical recommendation

- **Typical U.S. ecommerce store:** Run a serious comparison between **Stripe and Braintree**.
- **Shopify store:** Test **Shopify Payments** first, especially if you currently use an external gateway.
- **International or high-volume store:** Evaluate **Adyen**, with **Checkout.com** as another enterprise option.
- **Large business with recurring failures or multiple markets:** Consider a **multi-processor/orchestration strategy**, rather than relying on one provider. Braintree’s orchestration documentation specifically describes routing transactions to multiple PSPs/acquirers to improve authorization performance and geographic coverage. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/orchestration/overview/?utm_source=openai))

### Features I would require in an RFP

Ask each provider to demonstrate:

1. **Network tokenization** — issuer-recognized tokens that remain current when cards are replaced.
2. **Real-time and batch account updater** — particularly important for subscriptions and saved cards.
3. **Adaptive acceptance or smart retries** — not indiscriminate retries, which can increase network penalties.
4. **Detailed decline reporting** — issuer response, processor response, AVS/CVV results, 3DS status, and decline reason by BIN, issuer, country, device, and payment method.
5. **Risk controls you can tune** — so the provider’s fraud model does not block legitimate customers unnecessarily.
6. **3DS2 with risk-based exemptions** — authentication when useful, without forcing every customer through a challenge.
7. **Token portability** — the ability to migrate vaulted cards or use network tokens with another processor. Do not switch before confirming this; otherwise, many repeat customers may have to re-enter their cards. Braintree, for example, documents both “bring your own token” and forwarding options. ([developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com/braintree/docs/guides/network-tokens/getting-started?utm_source=openai))

### Before switching, diagnose the declines

Export the last 30–90 days of failed payments and segment them into:

- **Expired/replaced card:** account updater or network tokens should help.
- **Insufficient funds:** smart retries, customer emails, and alternative payment methods help.
- **AVS/CVV mismatch:** improve checkout data collection; don’t automatically reject every address mismatch.
- **“Do not honor” or generic issuer decline:** compare processor routing, fraud scoring, merchant descriptor, and 3DS handling.
- **3DS/authentication failure:** check whether your integration is incorrectly requiring 3DS for transactions that cannot complete it.
- **Gateway/processor errors:** switching providers or adding a backup route may materially help.

Also, don’t judge providers by their advertised overall approval rate. Run a **controlled pilot** using the same traffic, products, fraud rules, currencies, and checkout flow, then compare:

- authorization rate,
- false-decline rate,
- checkout conversion,
- 3DS challenge and failure rates,
- chargebacks,
- effective processing cost,
- subscription recovery rate,
- and support response time.

**If I had to choose a starting point without more details:** Stripe for a conventional U.S. store, Braintree if PayPal/Venmo and token portability matter, and Adyen if you operate internationally or at substantial scale.

| **Lowest fee for bank payments** | **Helcim or Square ACH** | Helcim: **0.5% + 25¢**, capped at $6; Square ACH: **1%, with caps depending on method** | Use ACH for invoices, subscriptions, or high-ticket services when customers accept it. ([helcim.com](https://www.helcim.com/pricing/?hcmSprt=1&utm_source=openai)) |

### My practical recommendations

- **You process under roughly $5,000–$10,000/month and want simplicity:** choose **Square**.
- **You process regular card volume or have average transactions above about $50–$100:** compare **Helcim** first; interchange-plus pricing may save money.
- **You run an online store or need an API:** compare **Stripe** and **Helcim**.
- **You primarily invoice customers:** consider **ACH through Helcim or Square**.
- **You need PayPal/Venmo as a customer payment option:** use PayPal for conversion and convenience, but avoid making it your only processor if fees are the priority.

### Important caveat

A processor with the lowest advertised percentage may not be cheapest overall. Compare:

1. Average transaction size  
2. In-person vs. online/card-not-present payments  
3. Monthly card volume  
4. ACH usage  
5. Hardware, software, chargeback, refund, and monthly subscription fees  

For example, on a **$50 in-person sale**, Square’s posted fee is about **$1.45**. Helcim may be lower, but its exact cost depends on the card’s interchange category and network fees rather than a single flat rate. Thus, **Square is usually the best low-volume/simple choice, while Helcim is often the better low-fee choice for established businesses willing to use interchange-plus pricing**.

For an online store, the main options are:

| Provider | Conventional digital wallets | Cryptocurrency payments | Best fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stripe** | Apple Pay, Google Pay, Link, and other regional wallets | Stablecoin payments, including USDC; customers can pay from supported crypto wallets and merchants can generally settle in fiat | Best all-in-one option for a custom store or Shopify-based setup |
| **PayPal** | PayPal, Venmo in the U.S., Apple Pay, Google Pay, and other wallets | “Pay with Crypto,” subject to merchant eligibility and market restrictions; PayPal can settle the merchant in local currency | Fast setup and broad consumer recognition |
| **BitPay** | Primarily crypto wallets rather than Apple Pay/Google Pay merchant checkout | Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, USDC, and other supported cryptocurrencies; supports Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento, and other platforms | Crypto-first stores wanting fiat settlement and reduced crypto exposure |
| **Coinbase Business** | Crypto-wallet checkout rather than traditional card wallets | Stablecoin and other crypto payments, payment links, APIs, and checkout tools | Businesses that want to accept and manage crypto directly |
| **Adyen** | Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal and many local wallets | Not generally a native cryptocurrency checkout provider; usually requires a separate crypto gateway | Large businesses needing global wallet and local-payment coverage |

**Practical recommendations:**

- Choose **Stripe** if you want Apple Pay/Google Pay plus crypto in a highly customizable checkout.
- Choose **PayPal** if you want the quickest setup and PayPal/Venmo alongside crypto checkout.
- Choose **BitPay** or **Coinbase Business** if cryptocurrency is central to your business; pair one with Stripe or Adyen for conventional wallets and cards.
- If you only need digital wallets—not crypto—**Adyen, Stripe, PayPal, and Checkout.com** are common choices.

Availability depends on your business country, customer location, supported currencies, industry, and compliance approval. Also, “crypto payments” may mean only stablecoins such as USDC rather than Bitcoin or every token. Stripe’s crypto checkout, for example, is focused on stablecoin payments, while BitPay supports a broader set of cryptocurrencies.
